problem: The answer says bitonic sort 'is shallower but uses more comparators' than odd-even transposition. This is false. For 8 keys bitonic uses 24 comparators while odd-even transposition uses 28, and in general bitonic size O(n log² n) is far smaller than the n(n−1)/2 comparators of the odd-even network. The answer also contradicts the worked example, where both networks have 6 comparators for n = 4.
fix: Bitonic: depth 6, size 24 comparators for n = 8. Odd-even transposition: 8 phases, 28 comparators (n(n−1)/2). Bitonic is shallower and for n ≥ 4 it uses no more comparators, and far fewer as n grows.

problem: The text says the median of the processors' local medians 'becomes the pivot, so the two halves are equal'. That is wrong. Only the true global median splits the data into two exactly equal halves. The median of the local medians gives each processor an approximately even split, so each subcube receives about half the keys, not exactly half. Q6 repeats the same claim.
fix: Each processor sorts its block and broadcasts its local median. The median of these p local medians is chosen as the pivot and broadcast along the hypercube. Each processor then splits its own block around the pivot and sends one part to the partner in the other subcube, so each half holds about n/2 keys even though the split is not exact. Q6 answer: the median of the local medians, because it makes each processor's split roughly balanced and keeps the two subcubes' workloads roughly equal.

problem: 'Odd-even merge sort has the same depth and size with a simpler merge' is too loose. Batcher's odd-even mergesort has the same depth, but it uses fewer comparators than bitonic sort (same O(n log² n) order, smaller constant). The odd-even merge network is usually considered more intricate than the bitonic merge network, not simpler.
fix: Odd-even merge sort has the same depth k(k+1)/2 and the same O(n log² n) size, with a smaller comparator count, but its merge network is more intricate than the bitonic merge.

problem: The step from 'all comparisons run together' to 'O(n) time' is not explained. With n² processors every pair is compared in one step, but each key still has to add up its n comparison results, and that summation is what sets the time (O(log n) with a tree, O(n) if each key's n results are added serially). As written, O(n) with n² processors looks inconsistent.
fix: It uses about n²/2 comparisons. On a CRCW machine with n² processors all pairs are compared in one step; the n comparison results of each key are then added, for example by a tree in O(log n) steps, giving O(log n) time with n² processors (O(n) time if only n processors are used).

problem: 'test 16 binary inputs, not one array' reads oddly; a beginner may think a 0/1 array is the only thing to test.
fix: For n = 4, test all 16 binary inputs instead of testing a few sample key arrays.

problem: The key term 'bitonic' is used but never defined, so the sentence 'makes a sequence rise then fall' is easy to misread as describing the whole algorithm rather than the sequences it builds.
fix: A bitonic sequence first increases and then decreases (cyclically, only one rise and one fall). Bitonic sort pairs elements with comparators in alternating directions to build bitonic sequences of length 2, 4, 8, …, then merges each bitonic sequence into a sorted one.
